question: Riddle time: I can blow bubbles but I'm not soap. I end up stuck under school desks. And in Singapore, shops aren't allowed to sell me. What am I?
topic: Weird laws and rules around the world
source_excerpt: The sale of chewing gum in Singapore has been illegal since 1992.

extra.why_interesting: Players think of a ban as something for drugs or weapons. Here it is a harmless sweet, and the reason (gum jamming metro doors and littering) makes it funny rather than sinister.
extra.verification_notes: Singapore has banned sale of ordinary chewing gum since 1992 (therapeutic gum excepted since 2004) and I found no repeal; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chewing_gum_sales_ban_in_Singapore.

explanation: Singapore banned ordinary chewing gum partly because vandals stuck it on the doors of its new metro trains and stopped them closing. Today you can only buy medical gum, from a pharmacy.

question: Fact or fiction: in Switzerland, it's against the law to keep just one guinea pig on its own.
topic: Weird laws and rules around the world
source_excerpt: guinea pigs may not be kept on their own

extra.why_interesting: It sounds like an invented 'crazy law' from an internet list, but it is real and has a kind reason behind it. There is even a Swiss service that rents out a companion guinea pig when one of a pair dies.
extra.verification_notes: Swissinfo's fact-check, citing the FSVO, confirms Swiss animal protection rules prohibit keeping guinea pigs alone (in force since 2008); no later change found.

explanation: Swiss law treats guinea pigs as social animals that get lonely, so they must have company. When one of a pair dies, some owners rent a stand-in friend so the survivor isn't left alone.

question: Finish this real British law: it is an offence to handle a certain fish 'in suspicious circumstances'. Which fish?
topic: Weird laws and rules around the world

extra.why_interesting: The wording sounds like a parody of legal language, and players picture someone suspiciously cuddling a fish. The real purpose, stopping trade in poached fish, makes it click.
extra.verification_notes: Section 32 of the Salmon Act 1986 is headed 'Handling salmon in suspicious circumstances'; the 2009 amendment I saw mentioned may have broadened it, but salmon remains the correct, well-known answer.

explanation: It comes from the UK's Salmon Act of 1986. Despite how it sounds, it targets people dealing in poached salmon, not anyone being strange with a fish.

question: In Longyearbyen, a town in Norway's far Arctic, the cemetery hasn't taken new burials for decades. What frozen reason is behind it?
topic: Weird laws and rules around the world
source_excerpt: Permafrost keeps remains intact for decades; new burials have effectively stopped since around the middle of the 20th century.

extra.why_interesting: The town is famous online for being a place where 'dying is banned'. Players can work out the real cause from everyday knowledge: things stay preserved in a freezer.
extra.verification_notes: Permafrost prevents decomposition, so Longyearbyen's cemetery has taken no coffin burials since about 1950; urn burials are allowed in special cases, a minor caveat (https://www.messynessychic.com/2018/03/26/the-town-where-its-illegal-to-die/).

explanation: The ground stays permanently frozen, so buried bodies barely decompose. Scientists have even recovered traces of the 1918 flu virus from victims buried there.
